query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor compositional modification by adding ~3–5 at.% Ti to a Mg-containing lightweight HEA promotes selective Ti segregation during non-equilibrium evolution, leading to the formation of a Ti-rich intermetallic network that directs the development of a protective TiO2-based oxide film under high-temperature oxidation, thereby improving corrosion resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast Mg-containing lightweight HEA (e.g. MgAlCuZnGd) in a metastable solid-solution state without Ti.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding a controlled amount (~3–5 at.%) of Ti during melting.
generation.conditions: Standard casting followed by ambient ageing, then exposure to high-temperature oxidation (700–800 °C) and subsequent corrosion evaluation (e.g. in NaCl solution).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a Ti-rich intermetallic phase network, particularly along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The preferential segregation of Ti during the evolution of the non-equilibrium state facilitates the in-situ formation of a passivating TiO2-rich layer during oxidation, which acts to reduce oxygen penetration and electrochemical attack, thus lowering corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ti-modified alloy will exhibit a significantly lower corrosion current density (by approximately 20–30%) and form a more protective, TiO2-dominated surface oxide compared to its Ti-free baseline.
generation.baseline: The original Mg-containing HEA without any Ti modification.
generation.boundary: The overall alloy density must remain below 6 g/cm³ and the Ti addition should not destabilize the desired phase balance.
generation.uncertainty: The possibility that Ti addition might also promote unwanted brittle phases if its solubility limits are exceeded.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples, one with the baseline composition and one with an additional 3–5 at.% Ti. Subject both to identical thermal histories and then expose them to high-temperature oxidation (700–800 °C in air). Follow with corrosion testing in a 0.1 M NaCl solution. Characterize the surface oxide composition using XPS and the phase distribution using XRD/TEM.
measurements: Corrosion potential and corrosion current density measurements
Surface oxide composition and thickness via XPS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-added alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance and formation of a predominantly TiO2-based oxide layer relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

papers.title: Modeling and Experimental Results of Selected Lightweight Complex Concentrated Alloys, before and after Heat Treatment.
papers.system: Al–Cu–Si–Zn–Mg and Al–Mn–Zn–Mg–Si lightweight alloy systems
papers.approach: CALPHAD, non‐equilibrium solidification and kinetic simulations paired with induction furnace casting and post-casting heat treatments
papers.findings: Identified multiphase structures where a solid solution forms initially (e.g., soft FCC) and subsequent diffusion‐driven precipitation leads to formation of intermetallic phases (e.g., Mg2Si, Al9Mn2Si). Differences in phase formation sequence were noted between alloys with different elemental concentrations.
papers.mechanism: Non‐equilibrium solidification followed by diffusion-controlled precipitation that produces a mixture of stabilized phases and secondary intermetallic compounds.

papers.title: Microstructure, Phase Formation and Heat-Treating of Novel Cast Al-Mg-Zn-Cu-Si Lightweight Complex Concentrated Aluminum Based Alloy.
papers.system: Al–Mg–Zn–Cu–Si complex concentrated aluminum based alloy (density ~2.63 g/cm³)
papers.approach: Gravity permanent mold casting combined with systematic heat treatments and microstructural characterizations
papers.findings: Demonstrated a precipitation transformation where the as-cast, metastable microstructure evolves via nano-scale secondary phase formation, affecting hardness, compressive strength, and oxidation behavior.
papers.mechanism: Controlled thermal processing drives the evolution from a metastable solid solution to an equilibrium state through precipitate nucleation and growth, dictating both mechanical and high-temperature behavior.

papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of MgTiZn and Mg₄TiZn Alloys After Ball Milling and Subsequent Spark Plasma Sintering.
papers.system: Mg–Ti–Zn alloys processed via high-energy ball milling and spark plasma sintering
papers.approach: Combination of mechanical alloying (ball milling) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) followed by XRD, SEM, STEM, and corrosion tests in NaCl solution
papers.findings: Both alloy compositions exhibited high hardness and significantly enhanced corrosion resistance (low corrosion current densities) due to formation of protective surface films. The Ti-rich oxide film was found especially effective in passivating the surface.
papers.mechanism: Non-equilibrium processing promotes the formation of intermetallic phases and a Ti-rich passivation layer at the surface that hinders corrosion propagation by acting as a physical barrier.

papers.title: First principles-based design of lightweight high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Quinary lightweight HEAs including systems such as Al–Be–Mg–Ti–Cu, Al–Be–Mg–Ti–Si, and Al–Be–Mg–Ti–Li
papers.approach: High-throughput DFT calculations, Monte Carlo simulations, and Grand Canonical Linear Programming (GCLP) free energy minimization
papers.findings: Identified top compositions with low density and high specific stiffness that are stable in a single solid-solution state only under metastable conditions; demonstrated that specific substitutions (e.g., Cu versus Si or Li) affect phase stability and propensity for compound segregation.
papers.mechanism: A competition between negative formation energies (driving solid solution stability) and kinetic effects (requiring fast cooling to freeze metastable states) governs the evolution of the alloy’s microstructure.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy (as a model for oxidation processes)
papers.approach: In situ and ex situ oxidation experiments at 400 °C using TEM, atom probe tomography, and XANES to reveal layered oxide formation
papers.findings: Observed formation of a multi-layered oxide film with distinct compositional zones (Ni-rich, Cr-rich, followed by a Fe/Co/Mn-rich layer) and noted that diffusion-induced defects play a role in film evolution.
papers.mechanism: Selective cation diffusion, driven by differences in redox potentials and atomic sizes, leads to compositional inversion and layered growth of protective oxide scales.

papers.title: Predictive multiphase evolution in Al-containing high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: Al_xTM systems (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi) within the HEA family
papers.approach: Combination of first principles calculations with Monte Carlo simulations to model order-disorder transitions and phase evolution
papers.findings: Reproduced experimentally observed order–disorder transitions and multiphase evolutions; highlighted that higher Al content can push the system into a partially ordered state above the melting point, while lower Al leads to solid-phase ordering near 1200 °C.
papers.mechanism: Diffusion and segregation processes during cooling govern peritectic reactions and ordering, which in turn dictate the balance between metastable solid solutions and intermetallic compound formation.

papers.title: Characterisation of a Novel Complex Concentrated Alloy for Marine Applications.
papers.system: Al–Cu–Si–Zn–Mg complex concentrated alloy designed for offshore/marine environments
papers.approach: Casting, heat treatment, corrosion testing, and microstructural analyses (SEM, XRD) to assess mechanical and corrosion properties
papers.findings: Revealed a multiphase microstructure with a primary dendritic α–Al phase and interdendritic intermetallic phases (e.g., Al2Cu) that contribute to high compressive strength and lower corrosion rates compared to conventional steel.
papers.mechanism: A uniform distribution and fine tuning of intermetallic phases coupled with alloying element effects promote passivation and mechanical reinforcement, thereby affecting corrosion and oxidation performance.

established: Non-equilibrium processing (casting, rapid cooling, ball milling/SPS) can trap metastable solid-solution states that later evolve into mixtures of solid solutions and intermetallic compounds.
Alloy composition, particularly the content of reactive constituents like Mg, Ti, and Al, strongly influences both phase evolution and the formation of protective oxide films.
Protective surface films (e.g., Ti-rich or Cr-rich oxides) formed during oxidation are critical for enhancing corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Computational methods (CALPHAD, DFT, Monte Carlo) have been successfully applied to predict phase stability and transformation pathways in lightweight HEAs and CCAs.

approaches_tried.approach: Induction melting with controlled casting and subsequent heat treatments
approaches_tried.outcome: Successfully produced lightweight alloys with designed multiphase structures, though some discrepancies between predicted and observed phases remain.

approaches_tried.approach: Mechanical alloying using high-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering
approaches_tried.outcome: Enabled the formation of refined microstructures and metastable phases that enhance corrosion and mechanical properties, particularly via the formation of passivating oxide layers.

approaches_tried.approach: First principles and Monte Carlo simulations for phase prediction
approaches_tried.outcome: Provided insight into the thermodynamic and kinetic factors controlling metastability and phase evolution, although experimental validation is sometimes limited by processing uncertainties.

mechanisms: Diffusion‐driven precipitation during non-equilibrium solidification leading to a mixed microstructure of solid solutions and intermetallic compounds.
Kinetic freezing of metastable phases via rapid cooling or mechanical alloying to capture non-equilibrium states.
Formation of protective passivation layers (e.g., Ti-rich, Cr-rich oxides) during oxidation due to selective cation diffusion influenced by redox potentials and atomic size mismatches.
disagreements: Some discrepancies are noted between CALPHAD/simulation predictions and experimental phase compositions, indicating challenges in accurately modeling multicomponent, reactive systems.
Differences in predicted stability of ordered versus metastable solid-solution states across computational studies versus experimentally observed phase segregations.
open_questions: How do the metastable states in non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEAs evolve under long-term exposure to corrosive and high-temperature oxidation environments?
What is the precise interplay between intermetallic phase distribution and the formation/maintenance of a protective surface oxide layer in these alloys?
How can processing parameters be optimized to consistently achieve the desired balance between solid solution and intermetallic phases for targeted functional properties?
opportunities: Investigate combinations of rapid cooling/ball milling with controlled heat treatments to 'freeze' desired metastable microstructures that optimize both corrosion resistance and high-temperature stability.
Explore alloy designs that incorporate strategic additions (e.g., Ti, Cr) alongside Mg to enhance passivation layer formation while maintaining low density.

Integrate first principles prediction with in situ experimental monitoring of phase evolution and oxidation to refine processing routes and guide alloy design in underexplored regions of the lightweight HEA phase diagram.

directions.direction: Use rapid cooling and controlled thermal treatments to freeze a non-equilibrium metastable solid solution that subsequently undergoes diffusion‐driven precipitation.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the non-equilibrium state that subsequently evolves into a mixture of solid solution and intermetallic phases. Evidence indicates that diffusion‐driven precipitation plays a key role in such alloys (see PMC7579168::web::035 and PMC9100001::web::004). It is feasible with rapid casting followed by sub‐critical annealing, and it can be linked to both corrosion and high‐temperature oxidation performance.

directions.direction: Tailor alloy composition by incorporating minor additions (e.g., Ti) to promote selective elemental segregation and intermetallic formation that catalyze the formation of protective passivating oxide layers.
directions.assessment: Directly addresses the design constraint (density below 6 g/cm³) and the need to manage differences in constituent properties. Prior work shows that reactive elements such as Ti can promote the formation of passivating surface films (cf. PMC10728166::web::052 and PMC12299034::web::007). The concept is supported by known physics of selective cation segregation and passivation, and is feasible experimentally.

directions.direction: Apply a controlled post-casting heat treatment to trigger a structural transformation from a metastable solid solution into a balanced microstructure with fine, uniformly distributed intermetallic precipitates.
directions.assessment: This intervention is well supported by studies that link thermal processing to precipitation behavior (see PMC9100001::web::004 and PMC7579168::web::037). By controlling the nucleation and growth of secondary phases, the microstructure can be tailored to affect both high-temperature oxidation and corrosion resistance. It directly addresses the evolution pathways from metastable states.

directions.direction: Conduct in-situ oxidation and corrosion studies to directly monitor the surface segregation and oxide scale formation dynamics during environmental exposure.
directions.assessment: This direction directly probes the evolution pathways and transient phenomena that mediate the corrosion and oxidation responses. Advanced in-situ techniques (e.g., environmental TEM, APT) have been successfully used in similar systems (see PMC11169556::web::008). Although technically challenging, the approach can provide direct mechanistic insights that relate microstructural evolution to functional performance.

candidates.intervention: Apply a sub-critical annealing treatment (300–500 °C for ~1 hour) to trigger controlled diffusion without complete equilibrium.
